hints: Think about what happens to cells in a tissue over time or after an injury - what state are the old cells in and what does the tissue need to keep working?
walkthrough:
What Repair Really Means**
Think of a tissue like skin or gut lining. Cells are constantly getting worn out, damaged or dying. Repair does not mean fixing an individual cell, it means making new identical cells by mitosis to take the place of those lost.
Final answer: Repair means replacing cells that are damaged, destroyed, worn out or old by mitosis to maintain tissue function.

hints: Start from normal control of the cell cycle - what normally stops cells dividing too fast or piling up?
Now think what goes wrong in a tumour cell - what causes the loss of control and what fails to stop faulty cells?
walkthrough:
Start With Loss of Control**
A fully differentiated cell should rarely divide. Tumour formation starts with a mutation, for example activation of an oncogene or inactivation of a tumour suppressor gene. That breaks the normal regulation of the cell cycle.

Describe How Division Is Abnormal**
Pick two clear features. The cell cycle becomes short, fast and continuous with faulty checkpoints, so errors are not checked. There is no contact inhibition, no response to signals to stop, and no apoptosis, so cells keep piling up and may lose their original function and spread.

Final answer: Any two from: result of mutation e.g. proto-oncogene to oncogene; shorter / faster / continuous cell cycles; no contact inhibition so division continues beyond space available; normal cell cycle checkpoints do not occur; loss of normal function; no response to cell signalling; no apoptosis.

hints: Recall what happens to the very ends of chromosomes each time DNA is replicated - is the copy always complete to the tip?
Think about what telomeres are made of compared to genes - if a bit is lost each cycle, why is it safer to lose telomere than gene DNA?
walkthrough:
Why Ends Get Shorter**
On the lagging strand DNA polymerase cannot copy right to the very end, so a few nucleotides are lost from the telomere after every replication. Telomeres are repetitive non-coding DNA with no genes.

Why Long Is Better for Stem Cells**
Adult stem cells must divide many times through life. Long telomeres act as a disposable buffer that protects the chromosome ends and the genes inside. Only after many cycles would shortening reach important genes, so long telomeres allow a long lifespan and many mitoses.

Final answer: After each cell cycle / DNA replication telomeres shorten, so long telomeres allow many more replications before coding DNA is lost; telomeres are non-coding and protect chromosome ends, so genes are not lost.

hints: Look at Fig. 4.1 and compare what HSCs can do at the top with what GMP cells can do below - how wide is the range of products?
Recall the two defining stem cell properties from the stem: self-renewal and ability to form the functioning cells of the tissue - which arrows are missing for GMP?
Check the key and the labels - GMP cells are shaded as progenitor cells and already sit part-way down one branch, so what does that tell you about differentiation?
walkthrough:
What Makes an HSC a Stem Cell**
HSCs are undifferentiated. They show self-renewal in Fig. 4.1 by dividing to make more HSCs, and they are multipotent, able to form all branches - CMP and CLP routes to red cells, platelets, neutrophils, monocytes, B and T lymphocytes.

Why GMP Fails the Test**
GMP cells are shaded as progenitor cells. They are already part-way differentiated down the CMP branch. They do not self-renew to make HSCs.

Limited Potency**
Unlike HSCs, GMP cells cannot make all blood types. Fig. 4.1 shows they only lead to two fates: immature neutrophils and immature monocytes. That restricted potency plus lack of self-renewal means they cannot be called HSCs.

Final answer: Any three from: GMP cells have already started differentiation / are partly specialised; show no self-renewal to produce HSCs; cannot form all blood cell types; only form immature neutrophils and monocytes.

hints: Monocytes leave the blood and enter tissues to carry out phagocytosis like neutrophils - what is the large tissue phagocyte called?
walkthrough:
Follow the Monocyte Path**
Neutrophils are phagocytes. Monocytes in blood migrate into tissues and differentiate into the large tissue phagocytes with the same engulfing function. Those cells are macrophages.
Final answer: X is macrophages.

hints: Think about the end of the B-lymphocyte line after immune response - which cell secretes Y-shaped molecules with specific antigen binding sites?
walkthrough:
Link Y to Humoral Immunity**
Mature B-lymphocytes, after immune response, become plasma cells (Y). Plasma cells secrete soluble proteins with specific antigen binding sites that bind antigen in humoral immunity. Those are antibodies, also called immunoglobulins.
Final answer: Molecules are antibodies / immunoglobulins.

hints: Think where T-lymphocytes go after the thymus and what they would meet all over the body if they were allowed to leave.
Consider what a T-cell receptor that fits a self-antigen would do if it met a normal body cell displaying that antigen.
Extend that to a full immune response - what lasting damage would follow if those self-reactive cells survived and formed memory?
walkthrough:
Self Antigens Are Everywhere**
Self-antigens are normal membrane proteins on your own body cells. After the thymus, T-lymphocytes enter the general circulation where they would constantly meet these self-antigens.

Danger If Self-Reactive Cells Escape**
If a T-lymphocyte that binds self-antigen were released, it would treat body cells like pathogens and become activated. Only lymphocytes that respond to foreign / non-self antigens should be left to survive.

Preventing Autoimmunity**
Activation would destroy healthy body cells, for example by T-killer attack, T-helper cytokine enhancement, phagocytosis or antibody attack, and would create memory T-cells for a faster attack next time. Destroying self-reactive cells in the thymus by clonal deletion prevents this autoimmune response.

Final answer: Any three from: T-lymphocytes are released into blood / circulation after thymus; if self-reactive cells were released they would be activated by self-antigens on body cells and trigger an immune response against body cells; leading to destruction / killing of body cells / autoimmune disease; including formation of memory T-cells and enhancement by T-helper cytokines / killing by T-killer cells.
